passages.title: Cosmic upheaval reveals every soul's record
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are the thunderous opening of Sūrah al-Infiṭār, and they work as a single sentence. Four "when" clauses pile up — the sky splitting, the stars scattering, the seas bursting, the graves overturned — and then the sentence lands on its answer in ayah 5: *then each soul will know what it has sent forth or left behind*. The cosmic upheaval is not described for its own sake. As Ibn Kathir puts it with deliberate brevity, "when this happens, then this will occur": every image exists to deliver that final line. On that Day, nothing about your life will remain hidden from you.

## A sūrah the Prophet ﷺ singled out

Ibn Kathir opens the virtues of this sūrah with a narration recorded by An-Nasa'i from Jabir: Muʿādh once stood and led the people in the night prayer, and he made his recitation long. So the Prophet ﷺ said, "Are you putting the people to trial, O Muʿādh? Why don't you recite 'Glorify the Name of your Lord the Most High' (87), 'By the forenoon' (93), and 'When the heaven is cleft asunder' (82)?" Ibn Kathir notes that the basis of this hadith is found in the Two Sahihs, though the mention of "When the heaven is cleft asunder" appears only in An-Nasa'i. So this was among the sūrahs the Prophet ﷺ himself recommended for leading people in prayer — a recitation that would not put the congregation to trial.

Ibn Kathir then recalls a narration he had cited earlier, from ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever would be pleased to look at the Day of Resurrection *with his own eyes*, let him recite "When the sun is Kuwwirat" (81), "When the heaven is cleft asunder" (82), and "When the heaven is split asunder" (84). That is a remarkable claim about what these ayat do. They are not merely information about the Last Day; they are a window onto it. Reciting them is meant to be the closest thing in this life to *seeing* it.

## The four scenes, one by one

**Ayah 1 — the sky splits.** The word is *infaṭarat*. Ibn Kathir explains it simply: "it splits," and points to the parallel expression elsewhere in the Qur'an, "Whereon the heaven will be cleft asunder (*Munfaṭir*)" (73:18).

**Ayah 2 — the stars fall.** *Intatharat* — Ibn Kathir glosses it in one word: "fallen." The stars do not stay in their places; they come down.

**Ayah 3 — the seas burst forth.** Here Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities on *fujjirat*. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reports from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Allah will cause some of it to burst forth over other parts of it." Al-Hasan said the same, adding "and its water will go away." Qatādah said: "Its fresh water will mix with its salt water." The separation between sea and sea, sweet water and salt, is undone, and everything floods into everything else.

**Ayah 4 — the graves spill out.** *Buʿthirat*: Ibn ʿAbbās said it means "searched," and As-Suddī said the graves "will be moved and those who are in them will come out." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the whole sequence: the sky splits, the stars fall, the seas are poured forth so that the fresh and salt waters merge into one mass, and the graves are overturned so that the corpses emerge from them.

When all four of these have happened, there is nothing left to shield a soul from the truth about itself — which is exactly where ayah 5 lands.

## Ayah 5 — the point of it all

*"Then each soul will know what it has sent forth or left behind."* Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and deliberate: "when this happens, then this will occur." All four upheavals are the condition; this knowledge is the consequence.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the two halves of the phrase, and gives two ways of reading them:

**First reading:** "what he sent ahead" is the good or evil a person actually did in his life, and "what he left behind" is what he failed to do or refrained from doing. On that Day a person will know not only his deeds but his omissions. The record has two columns, and the empty spaces count.

**Second reading:** "what he sent ahead" refers to the acts a person did himself, while "what he left behind" refers to what he did not do himself but laid down as a custom in society. Maʿārif supports this with the Prophet's ﷺ reported teaching: whoever establishes a good tradition in Islam will have its reward and the equivalent of the rewards of those who act upon it after him, without theirs being diminished in any respect; and whoever establishes a bad custom in Islam will bear its responsibility and the responsibility of those who act upon it after him, without theirs being diminished in any respect. On this reading, your record does not close at your death. Every practice you set in motion keeps writing entries into your account long after the grave — until the graves themselves are overturned and the whole account is finally shown to you.

Maʿārif notes that the same idea appears elsewhere in the Qur'an: "Man will be informed of what he sent ahead and what he left behind" (75:13).

## Living it

The Prophet ﷺ gave the practical instruction himself: recite this sūrah, and recite it as one who would look at the Day of Resurrection with his own eyes. Its purpose is not to satisfy curiosity about the end of the world but to collapse the distance between now and then — so that a person looks at today's deed and asks the only two questions ayah 5 leaves standing: what am I sending ahead, and what am I leaving behind? The first question audits your deeds and your omissions. The second audits the customs and examples you set in motion, which will keep earning for you, or against you, when you can no longer act. Both columns are still open.

passages.title: What deluded you about your generous Lord?
passages.tafsir:
After five ayat describing the sky splitting, the stars scattering, and the graves overturned, the sūrah suddenly stops addressing the cosmos and addresses *you*: "O humanity! What has deluded you about your generous Lord?" Ayat 6–12 are a single movement of thought — one piercing question (ayah 6), the evidence that makes the question unanswerable (ayat 7–8), the real answer named aloud (ayah 9), and the quiet warning that everything is being written down in the meantime (ayat 10–12).

## A question that is not looking for an answer

Ibn Kathir is emphatic about how ayah 6 works. This, he says, is a **threat** — a rebuke — not a genuine inquiry. Some people, he notes, mistakenly read it as if the Most Generous were inviting man to offer the excuse, "Your generosity deceived me," as though naming Allah al-Karīm here were a prompt for a flattering defence. Ibn Kathir rejects this. The real sense is: "O son of Adam! What has deceived you about your Lord, the Most Generous — meaning the Most Great — so that you went forth disobeying Him, and met Him with what was unbefitting?" It is the question of a court, not a conversation.

Ibn Kathir supports this with a report that on the Day of Judgement Allah will say: "O son of Adam! What deceived you concerning Me? O son of Adam, what was your response to the Messengers?" The question of ayah 6, in other words, is a preview of the very question that will be put to each soul when the events of ayat 1–5 have come to pass.

Ibn Kathir also mentions, from al-Baghawi, that al-Kalbi and Muqatil said this ayah was revealed about al-Aswad bin Shariq, who struck the Prophet ﷺ and was not punished in retaliation — a man who took the delay of consequences as licence, which is precisely the delusion the ayah names.

## The answer is hidden inside the question

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the passage's most penetrating insight: the adjective *karīm* ("Generous, Gracious") is not decoration — it *points to the answer*. What deludes man about his Lord? His Lord's own generosity. Because Allah is Karīm, He does not punish a person the moment he sins. His provision continues; his health, comfort, and worldly pleasures are not cut off. Man then misinterprets this magnanimity, and so falls into deception. Had he thought rationally, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that same generosity would have produced gratitude and obedience, not impudence.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Hasan al-Basri: "How many humans are there whose faults are put by Allah under cover — He did not disgrace them — yet they do not appreciate it, and are deluded by His grace." The very concealment that should melt the heart is taken as permission to continue. This is delusion in its true shape: not ignorance of Allah, but a false inference drawn from His kindness.

## The evidence of your own body (ayat 7–8)

Why is the question unanswerable? Because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the sūrah's opening described the violent end of this world, and these ayat now turn to the *beginning* of each person — man knows his beginning and knows his end, and either one, honestly considered, should have kept him from straying "a hair's breadth" from his Lord's commands.

Ayah 7 unfolds creation in three verbs. *Khalaqaka* — He created you. *Fa-sawwāka* — then He fashioned you perfectly: Ibn Kathir explains, He made you complete, straight, balanced, in the best of forms; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that every limb and organ is well placed, in such harmony and symmetry that any deviation from this construction would leave the organs dysfunctional. *Fa-ʿadalaka* — then He gave you due proportion: a balance, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, granted to no other animal to this degree — and not only physical balance but a well-balanced disposition, drawn out of opposing elements within man himself.

Ayah 8 — "in whatever form He willed, He put you together" — Mujahid explained as resemblance: a child may take after the father, the mother, the paternal uncle, or the maternal uncle. Ibn Kathir cites here the hadith in the Two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah: a man came to the Prophet ﷺ troubled that his wife had given birth to a black boy. The Prophet ﷺ asked whether he had camels, what colour they were — red — and whether any had patches of grey. "Yes." "How did that happen?" "Probably an inherited strain." "Likewise," said the Prophet ﷺ, "this, with your son, is probably an inherited strain." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the wonder in the other direction: since all human beings share one basic structure, the billions of us might have looked identical — yet the Creator's mastery has given each person features so distinct that no one is confused with another.

Ibn Kathir seals this section with a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad (and also by Ibn Majah) from Busr bin Jahhash al-Qurashi: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spat in his palm, placed his finger on it, and related that Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, says: "O son of Adam! How can you escape Me when I created you from something like this? Then I fashioned you and balanced your creation until you walked between your two garments, and the earth holds a burial place for you. You gathered wealth and withheld it — until, when the soul reached the collarbone, you said, 'I will give charity now.' But how will there be time for charity?" The hadith compresses the whole passage into one image: a being made from a drop, strutting the earth, hoarding against a Day he pretends will not come, offering repentance only when the time for it has closed.

## The real cause, finally named (ayah 9)

Ayah 9 opens with *kallā* — "But no!" — sweeping aside every excuse the deluded soul might offer. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: what actually drives you to oppose the Most Generous and meet Him with disobedience is your rejection, *in your hearts*, of the Hereafter — the recompense and the reckoning. *Ad-Dīn* here means the Judgement, the requital of deeds. The diagnosis is precise: careless living is not really caused by confusion about Allah's generosity; it is caused by a quiet, practical disbelief that anything will ever be counted.

## And yet it is being counted (ayat 10–12)

The passage answers that hidden denial with fact: "Over you are certainly guardians — noble writers (*kirāman kātibīn*) — who know whatever you do." These are real angels, appointed over every person, watching and recording. Ibn Kathir draws the practical conclusion in a single sentence: there are noble guardian angels over you, "so do not meet them with evil deeds, because they write down all that you do."

## Living under the question

The passage leaves the believer with one discipline: never to read Allah's generosity backwards. Continued provision, uninterrupted health, and sins left uncovered are the *karam* of a Lord who delays — not the verdict of a Lord who does not see. The hadith of Busr bin Jahhash fixes the deadline: goodness postponed to the collarbone is goodness lost. And the closing ayat give the daily practice — to act, in private as in public, as one who knows that noble writers are present and that nothing done escapes their knowledge.

passages.title: The two destinies: bliss and blazing Fire
passages.tafsir:
## The parting of ways

These four ayat set out the two destinies toward which every human life is heading: the righteous in bliss, the wicked in a blazing Fire. Ayat 13–14 announce the two outcomes side by side; ayat 15–16 then dwell on the second, pressing home that for the wicked the Fire is entered on the Day of Recompense and never afterwards escaped.

## Why these verses come here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the structural point that unlocks the passage: ayat 13–14 are connected back to ayah 5 of the sūrah — \"then one will know what he sent ahead and what he left behind.\" That earlier verse tells us that on the Day of Reckoning each person will know what he has done, and what the consequences of those deeds will be. Ayat 13–16 now spell those consequences out: perfect bliss for the righteous, the Blazing Fire of Hell for the sinners.

## Two words, two peoples

The Qurʼān names the two parties with two contrasting terms. In ayah 13 they are **al-abrār** — rendered in the sources as \"the righteous believers,\" or simply \"the virtuous.\" Ibn Kathir defines them not by a title but by a relationship: they are \"those who obeyed Allah and did not meet Him with disobedience.\" Righteousness here is measured by how one arrives before Allah — what state one is in at the meeting. Opposite them in ayah 14 stand **al-fujjār**, the wicked or sinners, whom Ibn Kathir says will be \"in Hell and eternal torment.\" There is no third category named between them.

## Entering the Fire — and never leaving it

Ayah 15 turns to the fate of the fujjār: *yaṣlawnahā yawma d-dīn* — \"burning in it on Judgment Day.\" Ibn Kathir renders the sense as \"therein they will enter, and taste its burning flame,\" and explains that *yawm ad-dīn*, the Day of Recompense, means \"the Day of Reckoning, Recompense, and Judgement.\" The Fire is not merely a place they are assigned; it is something they will enter and taste.

Then ayah 16 closes the door: *wa-mā hum ʿanhā bi-ghāʾibīn* — \"and they will have no escape from it,\" literally, they will not be *absent* from it. Ibn Kathir's explanation of this single phrase is the most sobering line in the passage: they will not be absent from the torment \"for even one hour.\" The torment will not be lightened for them; they will not be granted the death they will be requesting; they will have no rest — \"not even for a single day.\" Every ordinary form of relief — pause, reduction, escape, even annihilation — is negated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion in one word: the inmates of Hell will never be able to get away from it, because the torment will be *eternal*.

## Does this shut out intercession?

Commenting on ayah 16, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a question the reader may feel. The verse's finality is confirmed, it notes, by the sūrah's concluding assertion that on that Day no one will have power, of his own free will, to do anything for another — so is intercession (*shafāʿah*, one person pleading with Allah on behalf of another) denied altogether? The answer given is no. What is negated is anyone acting by his own free will and power on that Day. Intercession remains real, but only within Allah's permission: it happens when Allah grants someone leave to intercede for another, and then Himself accepts that intercession — and all matters, on that Day, will belong to Allah alone. Ibn Kathir says the same: no one will be able to benefit or rescue anyone else \"unless Allah gives permission to whomever He wishes and is pleased with.\" He cites here a saying of the Prophet ﷺ addressed to his own clan: \"O children of Hashim! Save yourselves from the Fire, for I have no power to cause you any benefit from Allah.\"

## What the passage asks of us

The passage offers only two destinations — bliss, or a blazing Fire with no absence, no lightening, and no exit. That sight is meant to make the believer take Ibn Kathir's definition of the abrār personally: to obey Allah, and to be careful not to meet Him carrying disobedience. And the Prophet's ﷺ words to Banū Hāshim turn that into a single imperative each of us can act on now, while the decision still lies ahead: save yourself from the Fire.

passages.title: The Day when no soul can help another
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Sūrah al-Infiṭār. Allah asks a question twice — "What will make you realize what Judgment Day is?" — and then gives the answer Himself: it is the Day on which no soul possesses anything for another soul, and the decision belongs entirely to Allah.

## Why the question is asked twice

In ayah 17 Allah says, "What will make you realize what Judgment Day is?" — and then in ayah 18 He repeats it: "Again, what will make you realize what Judgment Day is?" Ibn Kathir explains that this question is a **magnification of the affair of the Day of Judgement**; then, he says, Allah affirms it by repeating the question, and then explains it Himself in the ayah that follows.

The Day being asked about has already been named in this passage. Ayah 15 said the wicked "will enter and taste its burning flame *on the Day of Recompense*" — the same phrase, *yawm al-dīn* — which Ibn Kathir glosses as "the Day of Reckoning, Recompense, and Judgement". On ayah 16 he adds that its inmates "will not be absent for even one hour from the torment": it will not be lightened, nor will they be granted the death they will be requesting, nor any rest — not even for a single day. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same connection: the inmates of Hell will never be able to get away from it, because the torment will be eternal, "as the concluding verse of the Surah asserts" — the very verse now before us.

## Ayah 19: no soul can avail another

"It is the Day no soul will be of any benefit to another, and the decision that Day will be with Allah."

Ibn Kathir explains the first half plainly: **no one will be able to benefit anyone else, or help him out of that which he will be in — unless Allah gives permission to whomever He wishes and is pleased with.** Nothing moves except by Allah's leave.

Ibn Kathir illustrates this with the Prophet's ﷺ own words to his nearest relatives: "O children of Hashim! Save yourselves from the Fire, for I have no power to cause you any benefit from Allah." (Ibn Kathir notes he cited this report earlier, in his commentary on Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:214.) If even the family of the Messenger ﷺ were told by him that he possessed nothing for them before Allah, then kinship by itself will carry no one on that Day — each must save himself from the Fire.

## Does this negate intercession?

A careful reader may ask: if no soul can do anything for another, what of the intercession (*shafāʿah* — pleading on someone's behalf) that the believers hope for? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses this directly: the verse **does not negate intercession**, because intercession on that Day will not happen by anyone's own free will. It occurs only when Allah first grants someone permission to intercede on another's behalf, and then Himself accepts that intercession. Maʿārif's own rendering of the ayah carries this nuance: "A Day when no one — with his own free will in the Plain of Gathering — will have power to do anything for another." This matches Ibn Kathir's qualifier — "unless Allah gives permission to whomever He wishes and is pleased with." And all matters, on that Day, will belong to Allah alone.

## "And the decision, that Day, will be with Allah"

The closing clause — *wa-l-amru yawmaʾidhin lillāh* — is the sūrah's final word, and Ibn Kathir reads it alongside its sister verses: "Whose is the kingdom this Day? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!" (40:16); "The sovereignty on that Day will be for the Most Gracious" (25:26); and the verse every believer recites in al-Fātiḥah, "The Only Owner of the Day of Recompense" (1:4).

But is the decision not Allah's already, here and now? Ibn Kathir relays the answer of Qatādah: "By Allah, the Decision is for Allah today (now), but on that Day no one will try to dispute with Him about it." The decision is His in both worlds; what that Day removes is any disputing with Him about it.

## Living under this ayah

The passage leaves the believer with the sober, practical word the Prophet ﷺ pressed upon his own family: **save yourselves from the Fire**, for he told even them, "I have no power to cause you any benefit from Allah." And since intercession itself flows only from Allah's permission and His acceptance, hope on that Day rests with Him alone, to whom every matter belongs.

With this verse the sūrah ends. As Ibn Kathir closes: all praise and blessings are due to Allah, and He is the Giver of success and freedom from error.
